## the combination
a storm is a thing that has to break. a throne is a thing that has to hold.
you are one being asked to be the other , and that is the whole architecture of
your life.
your sun sits in the sixth mansion, where the old sky-watchers put the fierce work — the hunt,
the siege, the star of the howling god. it is the part of you that has to break the surface
of a thing and find out what it actually cost. you ask the question nobody at the table
wants asked, and you ask it at full volume, and you are usually right.
your moon sits in the tenth, on the brow of a lion and the seat of a king. that is the part of
you that has to keep its bearing. even at rest there is a carriage to you, a straightened spine,
an instinct not to be seen flinching. people bring you their best behaviour and save
their mess for someone else, because you have always looked fine.
>>
so the storm has to be conducted from a chair. you were built to break things open and
built to look composed while doing it — and neither one will let the other go.
this is why the two most common things said about you contradict each other. that you are
too much , and that you are hard to read . both are true. the voltage is real and
so is the composure, and you have spent a long time running one through the other, which is
exhausting in a way that does not show — because not showing is the other half of the
machine.
what it makes you unusually good at: walking into a difficult room and being the only person
who both names the problem and does not seem frightened by it. that is a rare pairing and people
build things around it. what it costs you is that nobody checks on the person who never
looks like they need checking on.

## the sixth mansion
參宿
alhena · the twins' foot
The Storm
4°17′ – 17°09′ gemini your sun stands here
every tradition that looked at this stretch of sky saw something that cannot be taken
back.
[sk] arabia

into a camel's neck to say whose it is. permanent by design.
[sk] india

the howler, the storm god, and its emblem is a teardrop.
[sk] china
參 Shēn — Orion entire, in the quarter of
the White Tiger. its animal is the ape: the long-armed caller of the canopy,
heard across miles before anything sees it.
a brand, a storm, and a voice that arrives before the body. the medieval election books gave
this mansion the fierce jobs — hunting, sieges, the work done at full force — and their reasoning
was simple: this is the stretch of sky for things that do not have an undo.
to be born under it is to be built for irreversibility. you go all the way in. you say the thing
out loud. and the mark you leave on a room stays on it after you have gone, which is a gift when
you meant it and a debt when you did not.

## the tenth mansion

the way a court files past a chair.
[sk] arabia

the brow of a beast so large it sprawled across a third of the sky.
[sk] india

royal throne. but its deity is not a king — it is the ancestors, the dead who are

[sk] china

Vermilion Bird. and here they part ways: china fixes it not on the lion but on
Alphard, the serpent's heart , in Hydra.
two civilisations looked at these degrees and saw the seat of a king. one looked at the same
degrees and saw the heart of a water-snake. the disagreement is old and nobody has ever
settled it , and you were born on the ground they were arguing over.
but the Indian reading is the one that turns the whole mansion, because it refuses the obvious.
the seat is real — and its god is the ancestors . the chair was carved before you
arrived. that is what a throne-born moon carries: authority handed over rather than
taken, and the private, unending question of whether you are worthy of a thing you did not build.
>>
the old books gave this mansion trade, alliance, and building. agrippa says it
“strengthens buildings.” it is the sky of the things meant to outlast the
person who made them.

## the combination
the arabs saw a lion here so enormous it took up a third of the sky. your sun is on
its eye . your moon is on its tail .
you are both ends of the same animal.
the eye is al-ṭarf — the glance, the look itself. it is the part of you that
wants to know the thing nobody announced : the pause before the answer, the name
that stopped getting mentioned, who stopped being cc'd. you read rooms at a resolution most
people do not have, and you have been doing it so long you no longer notice you are doing it.
and what you see, you keep. china put a willow on this stretch — the tree that bends and
trails and never quite lets go of the water. india called it the embrace , the coiled
serpent. three cultures, three images of holding on.
the tail is al-ṣarfa , the turning — the star whose rising the old
almanacs said broke the back of the summer heat. its animal is the snake, which grows only by
shedding, and its keeper is mars, which has no patience. your inner life molts.
it does it on a schedule that is nobody's business but yours, and it does it suddenly.
>>
so you hold everything, and then you let go all at once. the eye grips. the skin sheds.
there is nothing in between.
this is why people around you say the same sentence: you never said anything. and they
are right, and you were saying it for months. you do your grieving in advance and your
announcing at the end. by the time you speak, the decision is a year old and completely
finished — and to everyone who was not watching the weeks before, it looks like it came out of
nowhere and it looks cold.
it is not cold. it is the cost of a chart that notices everything and shows nothing until the
molt. what you are unusually good at is knowing, long before anyone else, that a thing is
over. what it costs you is that no one ever gets a warning, including the people who
would have changed if they had one.

## the combination
your sun is the beat everyone else keeps time to. your moon is the star that walks
behind something and never catches it. you set the rhythm from the second row.
india heard percussion in the twenty-third mansion — dhaniṣṭhā , whose emblem is a drum.
its guardian is the bat, the animal that finds a pitch-black world by making a sound and listening
to what comes back. that is the exact shape of it: you find out where you are by putting
something out and reading the return. groups organise their pace around you and almost
none of them have noticed they are doing it.
your moon sits on aldebaran , and the arabs named that star for what it does
rather than what it is. al-dabarān means the follower : it rises just
behind the pleiades and chases them across the sky every night, forever, without closing the gap.
>>
and here is the fact the name never mentions. aldebaran is far brighter than any star in the
cluster it follows.
so you are behind something on purpose. a person, a standard, a version of this you saw once and
cannot unsee — and you outshine it, and the arrangement suits you, and you would rather
not discuss it.
put the two together and you get something specific: the one keeping time is also the one who
declined the front. you can hold a room's tempo without ever being the reason the room is there,
and you prefer it that way, because standing behind is how you keep the sounding honest.
the cost is that a drummer does not get to be off-beat. your own slow week
registers to everyone else as the whole system faltering — and the person you are following has
no idea they are being used as a pace-setter by someone faster.

## the combination
the first mansion on the road, and the manger. you arrive first, and then
you feed whatever you found there.
your sun landed at the very front of aries — not merely early aries, but the first stretch
of the first mansion, the point the entire wheel is counted from. every degree of
sky anyone has ever measured is measured from somewhere near where your sun stood.
the desert astronomers called those two stars al-sharaṭān , the two
signs — the pair of horns that opened the year, the marker you watched for to know
the season had turned. india put the twin horse-headed physicians here: the gods' first
responders, the ones who arrive at the accident before anyone has finished calling for
help.
that is your hunger, and it is not ambition. you want to be there first —
before you are asked, before it is officially anyone's problem.
>>
and the cost is exact. arriving first and being ready are different skills, and this mansion
only gave you the one.
then the moon, at 0° cancer, on a patch of sky that is not really a star at
all — praesepe, a soft haze of hundreds of lights too faint to separate by eye. its
older latin name is the manger , and the two dim stars beside it were the donkeys
feeding there. india calls it puṣya , the nourisher , and gives it an
emblem you cannot misread: a cow's udder.
so the two halves of you finish each other's sentence. the gate gets you there before
anyone else. the manger is what you do once you have arrived. you are not the person who
turns up first to be seen turning up first. you turn up first because someone has to put the
kettle on.
the manger names the cost more bluntly than the gate does. feeders eat last and call it a
personality. you are not actually built to run empty — you have just gotten very
good at it, over a long time, and the goat that guards this mansion is the tell: the animal that
thrives on rocky ground nothing else wants. the room reads you as soft and files you
accordingly, and it takes people an embarrassingly long time to notice the spine.
a ghost-rooted moon is misjudged early and relied on
late. at seventy-six, you will know precisely how true that has been.
